title: The Killer (2023): A New and Somewhat Atypical Fincher Thriller

commenti.body:
\>We learn at the beginning that Fassbender’s character has no empathy

This was the problem I had with the film. If he were this uncaring character, >!then he wouldn't have a girlfriend he loves. !<

And the fact that they use the final line of the film to >!state he was actually "one of the many" is fucking ridiculous because we knew that twenty minutes into the film when the girl is revealed.!<

People who don’t have empathy don’t have to constantly tell themselves to not empathize with others. 

That’s a problem that I have with the movie. Fassbender plays the character as too cold when the entire narration is dedicated to him trying to detach himself from what he’s doing.

I thought it should have been played in a way where messing up on the shot  and killing an “innocent” basically sent him to confront the different parts of himself and his philosophy. The driver who is just doing his job, the handler who keeps telling him there is no point in fighting what he’s doing, the violence of the guy in Florida, the professionalism of Tilda Swinton, and finally the businessman at the end. 

That’s even why he doesn’t kill the money guy at the end because it will just lead him back in. He wants the money to stay away from him and not be a temptation.

Really this movie should have been about him becoming a human and escaping to love. It should have been filled with emotion. But instead it was just a cold and procedural like because that is Fincher’s style.

the audience knows he's a "normie" when he starts listening to the fucking Smiths lmao, his arc is him coming to terms with the fact that he isn't exceptional and is just like everyone else. why does it matter if the audience knows that already?

I read your substack article with interest, and subbed also. 

I would tend to agree with your general comments while disagreeing about the effectiveness of the scenario given as a thriller. 

If Fassbender is a sociopath truly without empathy, why does he care what happens to his partner? Why all the self-talk trying to convince himself that he's really such a stone-cold killer? Do stone-cold killers like songs about shyness and writing poetry to girls in Luxemburg? 

And if he's really a normie after all, why don't we ever come to care about him? Why does he commit murders like that of the taxi driver or the secretary without hesitation? 

For me the film is not convincing enough to be a serious thriller, and not wacky enough to be a satire. It sits uncomfortably in the middle and doesn't entertain much.  It could be a meta commentary on Fincher himself but that doesn't satisfy me much either. 

For a dead serious drama-thriller I'd prefer something like ***Le Samourai***, for a wild entertainment ***Leon*** or ***John Wick***, and for something quirky and whimsical, Ghost Dog.

But not always Fincher's style. ***Zodiac*** is extremely emotional both with regard to Jake Gyllenhaal's character, his wife Chloe Sevigny and his friend Robert Downey Jr. Though it is a highly procedural thriller, the core of the story is about the emotional toll all the murder has had on these people and even to some extent on the cop played by Mark Ruffalo.

Meanwhile ***Gone Girl*** is effective, I would argue, precisely because of the way Rosamund  Pike's psycho character impacts on the emotional mess of her husband Ben Affleck. He's flawed of course, selfish and dishonest, but has an emotional core that reacts strongly to his indignities and he cares a lot for his sister.

Eh, I’d say that Zodiac still handles the emotional toll of the story in a cold way. 

I’d also say that Gone Girl would have been more interesting if Rosamund Pike’s character wasn’t so hollow. One of the weirdest acting choices I’ve seen was for Pike to put on a some sort of femme fatale voice for that role. You got to play against expectations there and she didn’t. 

I mean, he does a lot of movies about people doing horrific acts. If he really went into the emotional reality of these stories, they’d be too grim to watch. Can you imagine watching Seven if it wasn’t done in Fincher’s detached style?

> People who don’t have empathy don’t have to constantly tell themselves to not empathize with others.
> 
> That’s a problem that I have with the movie. Fassbender plays the character as too cold when the entire narration is dedicated to him trying to detach himself from what he’s doing.

But that was what the point of the movie was for me.

The Killer is a very, very deadpan comedy. More so than a thriller. It's a film about the lies we tell ourselves in order to justify our existence, it's about the way assassins (and especially movies about assassins) lionise them in a way that makes them seem cool and superhuman, when here Fassbender's character is not only kind of shit at his job, but seems like a bit of a dolt.

He spends so much of the film justifying his actions and believing in his own exceptionalism and how he's different from everyone else, and yet the tools of his trade are some of the biggest corporations in the world - WeWork, McDonalds, Hertz, Amazon.

Every single mantra he repeats to himself - "Stick to the plan", "Only kill who you're paid to kill", "Empathy is weakness" - he breaks over the course of the film. His disguise is wearing a white linen suit and Hawaiian shirt. He calculates exactly how many minutes it will take for the Lawyer to die by nails to the lung, only for the man to die immediately on him. All of this is extremely funny to me, and I think it's meant to be.

Fincher has a very dark sense of humour, to the point where most of his films I would say are pretty damn funny. The Killer feels to me a bit like Fight Club in the way it's been misunderstood or misinterpreted, and if you watch it purely as a surface-level, John Wick or Jason Bourne-esque thriller, it's lacking. But to me he takes the pulpy "wronged assassin" genre and tries to elevate it by having the entire film and main character telling us it's one thing, but instead being something entirely different.

I'm not saying that means it works for everyone (the consensus I've seen online is that it's a mediocre film), and I personally think it's a minor Fincher work. But I still think it's more clever and interesting than it first appears to be, and perhaps is a victim of the glut of "badass assassins out for revenge" movies that have been made over the past two decades that people are taking it entirely at face value and IMO misinterpreting what it's actually doing.

Is he shit at his job? I don’t think so. He says he’s never made a mistake until the shot at the beginning. And we kind of can intuit that he’s not lying since we see the repercussions of failure. We then see him go through the film and get the upper hand on all these other supposed experts. 

He struggles against the guy in Florida, but that dude was more than twice his size! That’s not incompetence to beat someone that big. 

I agree that it could have been funny. We start out with this long monologue narration about his elaborate philosophy and about his expertise and then he fucks up and his whole cool, calm demeanor is broken and he can’t keep himself under control. The narration could have turned into the philosophy that he is fighting against at this point. That he had turned into an emotional monster. But that’s not how it’s played. It’s the same cold assassin throughout.

Those things are both features, not bugs. The audience is supposed to be able to tell that there's a "doth protest too much" thing going on with the constant affirmations. The payoff at the end is that he can let go of the inner conflict coming from doing a job that his conscience is clearly not suited for.

No, he's not *shit* at his job. Clearly not. But he's cultivated this self belief that he's this calculating, perfectly orchestrated killer, when in reality he fucks up multiple times. Including ending up in a fist fight with a guy who is a clear mismatch physically... he should never have ended up in that situation in the first place.

From your comments, it sounds like you wanted the film to me more about a guy's facade cracking and revealing the humanity underneath, whereas I don't think that's at all the kind of film Fincher is trying to make. His lack of "humanity", his willingness to kill, to affirm his reasons for killing, and even his unwillingness to kill the billionaire guy at the very end, all layer up to be a much broader critique of American exceptionalism, the icy pragmatism of capitalism, and the deeply damaged masculinity of modern America. These are themes that run through a great deal of his work - from The Social Network, to Zodiac, to Fight Club, to The Game. Which is why I think it's important to stand back from what the film is on the surface, or perhaps what it seems like a lot of people wanted or assumed it to be, and see what it's doing from a macro perspective.

Put it this way - if this was made in French by a French director, and yet was still set in America, I think the layers of critique of American society would've been much more obvious. But I think because it's made by an American, and someone who has a history in making films about serial killers, I think a lot of the intent around it has been missed.

It’s not about what I want from it, it’s about what I can figure out from what I saw. You’re saying that it’s not supposed to be about this guy changing, but he even sees himself as different in the end. He starts out by saying he is one of the few (before he messes up his shot) then in the end he is saying he is part of the many. I guess we’re supposed to write that off as bullshit even though you’re admitting that he goes against his philosophies multiple times after he messes up at the beginning?!?

He’s supposed to be reflecting on what he did and who he is. His wife or whatever getting almost killed mirrors the situation at the beginning of the movie. These hitman came to kill one person and ended up hurting someone else. His philosophy doesn’t allow for mistakes, something he thought he was incapable of before but now sees as a real possibility. 

This is what sets him on his journey. He’s told multiple times that it doesn’t make sense for a person like him to do these things because he’s got the money to disappear. He’s doing this stuff because he has to come to terms with himself in order to escape the life for love. 

It’s makes sense for all this to be there. If he’s just this cold, narcissistic sociopath, then his behavior doesn’t fit.
I mean Fincher has directed tens of music videos for rock music bands. The man enjoys The Smiths. It's not ironic.

Thank you for reading!

>For me the film is not convincing enough to be a serious thriller, and not wacky enough to be a satire.

I completely understand this outlook and your overall criticisms. I watched it with friends and we were expecting a run of the mill Fincher thriller but we were laughing at certain parts, which may be what caused me to like the movie more in that respect. If I watched it on my own c I could see how it feels uneven and like you said, a little uncomfortable.

>Le Samourai

Fincher did say that this was his main influence, so I wonder how he views The Killer — dark satire? To me it’s on the verge of something like HBO’s Barry but not nearly as silly or overtly comedic.

Just reading the comments here I believe that people are unclear about sociopathy.

Sociopaths are not incapable of caring. They may not experience love or affection the way a non sociopath does, but they can experience infatuation, jealousy, fascination. That combined with an obsession of power or control can create a very strong attachment or desire to "care for" or protect a person. 

There is nothing strange about The Killers motivation to get revenge and protect his girlfriend.
